# Matrices and condition numbers
 
## Introduction
When solving the system  $A\textbf{x}=\textbf{b}$ on a computer, the matrix $A$ and the right hand side $\textbf{b}$ will typically be subject to measurement- or roundoff-errors.
The computer will therefore really solve a problem on the form. 
$$(A+E)\textbf{y}=\textbf{b}+\textbf{e},$$
where $E$/$\textbf{e}$ is a matrix/vector with smalle elements, and which represent an error from the actual coefficient matrix/right hand side.
In what follows we will assume for simplicity that there are no errors in the coefficient matrix, so that $E=0$.

We will be concerned with how the error $\textbf{e}$ in the right hand side propagates to the solution of the system. 
Are there cases where even a small error $\textbf{e}$ propagates to a large error between the solutions $\textbf{x}$ and $\textbf{y}$? 
Such behaviour is clearly not desirable, since it makes us vulnerable w.r.t. small errors. 
To illustrate that such behaviour is possible, set
$$A=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1+\epsilon & 1-\epsilon \\ 1-\epsilon & 1+\epsilon\end{pmatrix},$$ 
where $\epsilon$ is a real number we will vary.

::: {#exr-1}
Show that the solution of the system 
$A\textbf{x}=\textbf{b}$, where $\textbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}$, is
$\textbf{x}= \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. 

::: {.content-visible when-meta="sols"}
We have that 
$$
A\textbf{x}= \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1+\epsilon & 1-\epsilon \\ 1-\epsilon & 1+\epsilon\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
= \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1+\epsilon+1-\epsilon \\ 1-\epsilon+1+\epsilon\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \textbf{b}.
$$
:::
:::

::: {#exr-2}
Find the eigenvalues of $A$, and the corresponding eigenvectors. 

::: {.content-visible when-meta="sols"}
We need to solve
$$\det(\lambda I -A) = (\lambda-(1+\epsilon)/2)^2 - (1-\epsilon)^2/4 = \lambda^2 - (1+\epsilon)\lambda + \epsilon.$$
This has roots
$$\frac{1+\epsilon \pm\sqrt{(1+\epsilon)^2   -4\epsilon}}{2}= \frac{1+\epsilon \pm(1-\epsilon)}{2}.$$
The biggest eigenvalue is $\lambda_1=1$, the smallest is $\lambda_2=\epsilon$. 
Let us find the eigenvectors.

* An eigenvector for $\lambda_1=1$.
$$
I-A = \begin{pmatrix} 1-(1+\epsilon)/2 & -(1-\epsilon)/2 \\ -(1-\epsilon)/2 & 1-(1+\epsilon)/2 \end{pmatrix} 
= \begin{pmatrix} (1-\epsilon)/2 & -(1-\epsilon)/2 \\ -(1-\epsilon)/2 & (1-\epsilon)/2\end{pmatrix}
\sim \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
$$
so that we can set $\textbf{v}_1=(1,1)$.
* An eigenvector for $\lambda_2=\epsilon$:
$$
\epsilon I-A = \begin{pmatrix} \epsilon-(1+\epsilon)/2 & -(1-\epsilon)/2 \\ -(1-\epsilon)/2 & \epsilon-(1+\epsilon)/2 \end{pmatrix} 
= \begin{pmatrix} -(1-\epsilon)/2 & -(1-\epsilon)/2 \\ -(1-\epsilon)/2 & -(1-\epsilon)/2 \end{pmatrix} 
\sim \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
$$
so that we can set $\textbf{v}_2=(1,-1)$.

:::
:::



If we have a small error $\textbf{e}$, we would expect that the solution of $A\textbf{y}=\textbf{b}+\textbf{e}$ is close to $(1,1)$, regardless of what $\epsilon$ may be.

::: {#exr-3}
Set $\textbf{e}=10^{-3}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$. Show that the solution of $A\textbf{y}=\textbf{b}+\textbf{e}$ is 
$$\textbf{y}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + 10^{-3}\epsilon^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}.$$

::: {.content-visible when-meta="sols"}
We have that $\textbf{y}=\textbf{v}_1 + 10^{-3}\epsilon^{-1}\textbf{v}_2$, so that 
$$
A\textbf{y} = A\textbf{v}_1 + 10^{-3}\epsilon^{-1}A\textbf{v}_2 = \textbf{v}_1 + 10^{-3}\textbf{v}_2 = \textbf{b} + \textbf{e}.
$$
:::
:::

Here something unexpected happened: When $\epsilon$ is big the solution $\textbf{y}$ is near the exact solution $\textbf{x}$, 
but when $\epsilon$ is small, this is not the case. 
What goes wrong here? The explanation we will give is that $A$ has a high *condition number* when $\epsilon$ is small. 
Put  differently, when $\epsilon\to 0$ the matrix $A$ gets close to the singular matrix $\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, 
and this is problematic since a system with a singular matrix does not give unique solutions.


Since the discussion above has to do with errors , we need to be precise about this.
When talking about the error between two quantities it is natural to use the concept of relative error:


::: {#def-condnumber}
If $a$ and $b$ are numbers, their relative error is defined as $\left|\frac{b-a}{a}\right|$.
If $\textbf{a}$ and $\textbf{b}$ are vectors, their relative error is defined as $\frac{|\textbf{b}-\textbf{a}|}{|\textbf{a}|}$.
:::

Relative error says more about the relationship between $a$ and $b$ than what the *absolute error* \index{Feil!absolutt} $|b-a|$ does, 
since it, contrary to the absolute error, doesn't change if we scale the numbers ($\left|\frac{cb-ca}{ca}\right|=\left|\frac{b-a}{a}\right|$ for any $c\neq0$).
The relative error also says something about how many decimals $a$ and $b$ have in common: If the relative error is approximately $10^{-k}$, 
you can expect that about the first $k$ decimal digits in $a$ and $b$ agree.
For the systems $A\textbf{x}=\textbf{b}$ and $A\textbf{y}=\textbf{b}+\textbf{e}$ above there are two different relative errors:

1. The relative error in the right hand side: $| (\textbf{b}+\textbf{e}) - \textbf{b}|/|\textbf{b}| = |\textbf{e}|/|\textbf{b}|$.
2. The relative error between the solutions $\textbf{x}$ og $\textbf{y}$: $|\textbf{y}-\textbf{x}|/|\textbf{x}|$.

The ratio 
$$ \frac{  |\textbf{y}-\textbf{x}|/|\textbf{x}| }{ |\textbf{e}|/|\textbf{b}| }$$ {#eq-forholdrelerr}
says how much the relative error in the right hand side propagates to the solutions. 
If this factor is about $10^{-n}$, it means that about $n$ decimal digits may be lost when solving the perturbed system. 


::: {#exr-4}
Compute the relative errors $|\textbf{y}-\textbf{x}|/|\textbf{x}|$ and $|\textbf{e}|/|\textbf{b}|$. What is the ratio @eq-forholdrelerr?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="sols"}
We have that
$$\textbf{y}-\textbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 + 10^{-3}\epsilon^{-1} \\ 1 - 10^{-3}\epsilon^{-1} \end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=10^{-3}\epsilon^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} 1\\-1 \end{pmatrix}$$
It follows that $|\textbf{y}-\textbf{x}|/|\textbf{x}|=10^{-3}\epsilon^{-1}$.
We also have $|\textbf{e}|/|\textbf{b}|=10^{-3}$, 
so that the ratio @eq-forholdrelerr is $\epsilon^{-1}$.
:::
:::

The previous exercise shows that the propagation factor @eq-forholdrelerr for relative error may be large. 
The following result, which we will not prove, states how big it may be.

::: {#prp-kondisjon-symmetrisk}
Suppose that $A$ is symmetric and invertible, and let
$$|\lambda_1|\geq|\lambda_2|\geq\cdots\geq|\lambda_n|>0$$
be the eigenvalues of $A$ listed with decreasing absolute value. Then we have that
\begin{equation} \label{condnumberineq}
\left|\frac{\lambda_n}{\lambda_1}\right| \frac{|\textbf{e}|}{|\textbf{b}|} \leq \frac{|\textbf{y}-\textbf{x}|}{|\textbf{x}|}  \leq \left|\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_n}\right|  \frac{|\textbf{e}|}{|\textbf{b}|}
\end{equation}
:::

The *condition number* of $A$ is defined as $K(A)=|\lambda_1/\lambda_n|$. With this notation \eqref{condnumberineq} can be written as
\begin{equation} \label{condnumberineq2}
\frac{1}{K(A)} \frac{|\textbf{e}|}{|\textbf{b}|} \leq \frac{|\textbf{y}-\textbf{x}|}{|\textbf{x}|}  \leq K(A) \frac{|\textbf{e}|}{|\textbf{b}|}.
\end{equation}
Note that 

* the right inequality says that the relative error in the right hand side propagates at most by a factor of $K(A)$ to the solution of the system,
* the left inequality can be rewritten as $\frac{|\textbf{e}|}{|\textbf{b}|} \leq K(A)\frac{|\textbf{y}-\textbf{x}|}{|\textbf{x}|}$. In this form it states that the relative error in $\textbf{x}$ 
propagates at most by a factor of $K(A)$ when performing the matrix multiplication $\textbf{b}=A\textbf{x}$.

::: {#exr-5}
What is the condition number of the matrix $A$?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="sols"}
The eigenvalues were $\epsilon<1$ and $1$, so that the condition number is $\epsilon^{-1}$. 
:::
:::

::: {#exr-6}
Let us change the right hand side to $\textbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\-1 \end{pmatrix}$, and the error to $\textbf{e}=10^{-3}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. 
Compute the same quantities as in Exercise 4. You can use that the new solutions are 
\begin{align*}
\textbf{x} &=  \epsilon^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 1\\-1\end{pmatrix} &
\textbf{y}&=\epsilon^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 1\\-1\end{pmatrix} + 10^{-3}\begin{pmatrix} 1\\1 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{align*}

::: {.content-visible when-meta="sols"}
That the stated $\textbf{x}$ and $\textbf{y}$ are correct can be verified as follows: 
\begin{align*}
A\textbf{x}&= \epsilon^{-1}A\textbf{v}_2 = \textbf{v}_2=\textbf{b} \\
A\textbf{y}&= \epsilon^{-1}A\textbf{v}_2 + 10^{-3}A\textbf{v}_1 = \textbf{v}_2 + 10^{-3}\textbf{v}_1 = \textbf{b} + \textbf{e}.
\end{align*}
We now get 
\begin{align*}
|\textbf{y} - \textbf{x}|/|\textbf{x}|&=10^{-3}\sqrt{2}/(\epsilon^{-1}\sqrt{2})=10^{-3}\epsilon \\
|\textbf{e}|/|\textbf{b}|&=10^{-3}\sqrt{2}/\sqrt{2}=10^{-3}. 
\end{align*}
The ratio @eq-forholdrelerr is thus $\epsilon$. 
:::
:::

We have thus shown that the $\textbf{b}$ and $\textbf{e}$ from Exercise 4 give maximal propagation of relative error ($\epsilon^{-1}$) when solving the system $A\textbf{x}=\textbf{b}$, 
while the $\textbf{x}$ and $\textbf{y}$ from Exercise 6 give maximal propagation of relative error when computing the matrix multiplication $\textbf{b}=A\textbf{x}$. 




The example above may seem rather obvious, since it is close to a singular matrix. 
There exist other matrices with high condition numbers, where this is less obvious. 
An example is the Hilbert matrix, which has elements $h_{kn}=1/(k+n-1)$. 
A $4\times 4$ Hilbert matrix can be created as follows.

```{python}
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(1,5).reshape((4,1))
1/(x + x.T - 1)
```
By writing \texttt{cond(A)} we get the condition number of $A$. 

::: {#exr-7}
Plot the condition number of the Hilbert matrix as a function of $n$, where $n$ goes from $14$ to $20$. 

::: {.content-visible when-meta="sols"}
You can also get an $n\times n$ Hilbert matrix with the command \texttt{hilbert(n)} in the package \texttt{scipy}.
The following code uses this.
```{python}
import scipy.linalg as scp
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

n = np.arange(20)
ch = np.zeros(20)
for k in n:
    ch[k] = np.linalg.cond(scp.hilbert(k+1))
plt.semilogy(n+1,ch)
```
This plot is logarithmic.
Along the $x$-axis we have $n$, along the $y$-axis we have the number of correct digits we lose.
We see that the Hilbert matrix loose $2$ digits precision when we increment $n$.
:::
:::
